When Bringing Your Baby Into the World Leaves You Feeling Shaken, Unheard, or Overwhelmed

Perhaps everyone around you keeps saying, "At least you and the baby are healthy", while inside, you feel shaken, grief-stricken, angry, or unable to stop replaying what happened during pregnancy, labour, or birth.

Maybe medical emergencies, unexpected interventions, intense pain, feeling dismissed or powerless, a Neonatal Intensive Care Unit (NICU) stay, or complications during pregnancy left your mind and body feeling unsafe long after returning home.

You may feel guilty for struggling when you expected to feel purely joyful, or find yourself dreading follow-up appointments, reminders of hospitals, or thoughts of future pregnancies.

Birth trauma is not defined solely by what is written on a medical chart. It is shaped by how overwhelming, frightening, or unsupported the experience felt to you: and it can affect birthing parents as well as partners who witnessed the event.

If these experiences feel familiar, you do not have to carry them quietly on your own.

With paced, compassionate psychological support, it is possible to process what you have been through and feel steadier in yourself and your parenting journey.

Could This Be What You're Experiencing?

Responses to pregnancy and birth trauma vary widely from person to person. Some parents experience vivid memories or heightened anxiety, while others feel emotionally detached, irritable, or weighed down by self-blame.

You may notice that you:

  • experience unwanted memories, flashbacks, or nightmares about pregnancy, labour, or hospital care
  • feel intense distress, a racing heart, or tension when seeing pregnant women, babies, hospitals, or birth stories
  • avoid medical check-ups, postpartum appointments, or conversations about your birth experience
  • feel persistently on edge, hyper-alert about your baby's safety, or unable to relax even when your baby is sleeping
  • carry deep sadness, anger, or grief over the birth experience you had hoped for
  • feel emotionally numb, disconnected from yourself, or unsure how you feel about bonding right now
  • struggle with guilt, self-blame, or wondering what you "could have done differently"
  • feel overwhelmed by the thought of intimacy, contraception, or future pregnancies

Experiencing these feelings does not mean you are failing as a parent. Similar responses can also overlap with postnatal anxiety, postnatal depression, sleep deprivation, or grief following pregnancy complications or loss.

A supportive, clinically informed consultation can help clarify what may be contributing to how you are feeling and what type of care may be appropriate.

You May Be Looking for Support Because...

Every parent and partner reaches out for perinatal trauma support at a different stage.

You may be seeking help because:

  • distressing memories or feelings from pregnancy or birth have not settled over time
  • you feel isolated when well-meaning friends or family focus only on the baby being healthy
  • anxiety around medical settings, feeding, or your baby's wellbeing is exhausting you
  • you are a partner or support person feeling shaken, helpless, or overwhelmed after witnessing a difficult birth
  • you are pregnant again, or considering another pregnancy, and feeling anxious about repeating past experiences
  • you have spoken with your GP or maternal health nurse about a Mental Health Treatment Plan and want a practitioner who understands perinatal trauma

You do not need to have everything worked out, or be ready to recount every detail of your birth, before reaching out.

Understanding Pregnancy & Birth Trauma

Why Subjective Experience Matters Most

A birth or pregnancy experience does not need to involve a life-threatening emergency to feel traumatic. Feeling frightened, unprepared, out of control, unheard by care providers, or separated from your baby can deeply overwhelm the nervous system.

When a threat or sense of helplessness occurs during such a vulnerable moment, the brain's survival system stores fragmented sensory and emotional memories. Later, everyday reminders, a hospital smell, a physical sensation, or a baby crying, can trigger the body to react as though the danger is happening again.

This is a protective nervous system response, not a reflection of your strength or capacity as a parent.

Trauma-informed perinatal therapy provides a safe, validating space to honour your experience without judgment and support your nervous system to settle at your own pace.

When Birth Trauma Affects Everyday Life

Unprocessed pregnancy or birth trauma can influence several areas of daily life during an already demanding transition.

Emotional Wellbeing and Grief

Carrying anger, disappointment, sadness, or shock alongside the everyday demands of caring for a newborn or young family can feel deeply isolating.

Sleep and Nervous System Rest

Even when opportunities to rest arise, hypervigilance, racing thoughts, or distressing dreams can make genuine relaxation difficult.

Medical Care and Future Planning

Avoiding postnatal check-ups, pap smears, dental visits, or discussions about future pregnancies is a common protective response to medical triggers.

Parenting Confidence and Self-Trust

Feeling as though your body or voice was not respected during pregnancy or birth can leave lingering self-doubt in everyday parenting decisions.

Physical Tension and Exhaustion

Holding unspoken distress in the body, alongside physical recovery and broken sleep, can contribute to persistent fatigue, muscle tightness, and overwhelm.

Every parent's story is unique, and support is always paced gently around your energy, baby's routine, and personal comfort.

When Birth Trauma Affects Partners and Family

How Perinatal Trauma Ripples Across Relationships

Pregnancy and birth are shared milestones, yet partners often experience the event from different vantage points, and may cope in very different ways afterward.

While one partner may want to talk through what happened or avoid reminders, the other may feel helpless, shut down, or unsure how to offer comfort while processing their own shock.

Over time, this can contribute to:

  • feeling disconnected or out of sync with your partner during the transition into parenthood
  • difficulty communicating about intimacy, medical appointments, or plans for future children
  • partners carrying silent distress or guilt after feeling powerless during labour or NICU care
  • tension with extended family when boundaries around visitors or birth stories feel crossed

Recognising these patterns is not about blame: it creates space for mutual understanding, gentler communication, and shared support.

You Don't Have to Figure It Out Alone

Safe, Paced, Evidence-Based Support Tailored to You

Perinatal trauma therapy is warm, collaborative, and paced around your readiness. You remain in control of what you share and when, with practical grounding and emotional safety prioritised from your very first session.

Depending on your individual needs and goals, therapy may focus on:

  • creating a validating space to have your pregnancy or birth experience heard without minimising your feelings
  • building practical nervous system grounding and calming strategies that fit into busy parenting routines
  • gently processing distressing birth memories using established, evidence-based approaches when you feel ready
  • exploring feelings of grief, anger, guilt, or self-blame with compassion
  • supporting confidence and emotional connection in your parenting role
  • preparing emotionally for medical appointments or considering a subsequent pregnancy
  • supporting partners or couples navigating the shared impact of a difficult birth

Support respects the realities of early parenthood, including flexible pacing and telehealth options from home.

What Could Change with the Right Support?

With tailored, trauma-informed psychological support, many parents and partners gradually feel steadier, more grounded, and more connected in everyday life.

Depending on your individual goals and circumstances, therapy may help you:

  • feel less overwhelmed when memories, anniversaries, or medical reminders arise
  • experience fewer or less intense flashbacks, nightmares, and physical tension
  • release unhelpful self-blame and grieve unmet expectations with self-compassion
  • feel calmer and more present during day-to-day moments with your baby and family
  • communicate your needs and boundaries more clearly with partners and health providers
  • approach future healthcare or family planning decisions with greater steadiness

Progress is individualised and gentle, and a supportive therapeutic relationship provides consistent care alongside the transitions of parenthood.

Small Changes Can Make Everyday Life More Manageable

Practical Grounding Steps Alongside Therapy

When caring for a baby or young family while carrying trauma responses, small, realistic anchors tend to be far more helpful than adding extra pressure.

Alongside professional support, many parents find it helpful to:

  • use brief present-moment grounding, such as feeling your feet on the floor, taking a slow exhale, or naming three things you see in the room, when memories intrude
  • give yourself permission to skip birth-story conversations or set gentle boundaries with visitors when feeling drained
  • lower non-essential household expectations so your energy goes toward rest, nourishment, and basic care
  • write down questions or preferences before medical appointments, or bring a trusted support person with you
  • remind yourself that two feelings can coexist: you can deeply love your baby while still grieving a painful or frightening birth
  • reach out to trusted peers or perinatal support networks so you do not carry your story in isolation

Strategies work best when adapted to your baby's routine, recovery needs, and personal preferences.

What Could Support Look Like?

Individualised Care for Parents and Partners

Because perinatal experiences touch physical recovery, emotional health, and family relationships, support is tailored around your circumstances and stage of parenthood.

Trauma-Informed Perinatal Psychological Therapy

Depending on your practitioner's training and your goals, evidence-based approaches, such as Trauma-Focused Cognitive Behavioural Therapy (TF-CBT), Eye Movement Desensitisation and Reprocessing (EMDR), Acceptance and Commitment Therapy (ACT), and compassion-focused approaches, may help support stabilisation and memory processing.

Partner and Couples Support

Dedicated sessions for partners, or joint couples sessions, can help both parents process their experience and strengthen communication during the postnatal period.

GP, Midwife, and Maternal Health Collaboration

Your General Practitioner (GP), obstetrician, midwife, or child health nurse oversees your physical postnatal care. Where appropriate and with your consent, your practitioner can liaise with your healthcare team, and your GP can also discuss a Mental Health Treatment Plan where eligible.

You Don't Need to Know Where to Start

Flexible Support Designed Around Early Parenthood

When you are juggling feeds, broken sleep, and appointments, arranging psychological support should feel calm, straightforward, and accessible.

You do not need to share graphic details of your birth during your initial enquiry, nor do you need to have everything worked out before contacting us.

At Michelle Barratt Psychology, our team listens gently to what you feel comfortable sharing and helps connect you with an appropriate practitioner.

Whether you are:

  • processing a recent difficult birth or pregnancy complication
  • navigating lingering birth trauma months or years later, or preparing for another pregnancy
  • a partner seeking support after witnessing a distressing birth
  • holding a GP Mental Health Treatment Plan and looking for a supportive fit
  • wanting in-person sessions in Brisbane or convenient online telehealth sessions from the comfort of home

we are here to help make taking that first step feel safe, respectful, and manageable.

Why Clients Choose MBP

Clinically Informed Support, With Families at the Centre

Michelle Barratt Psychology & Administration Services (MBP) provides a welcoming, neutral, and professionally managed entry point for parents and families seeking psychological and allied health care.

Clinically Informed Intake

Sensitive, respectful intake processes help us understand your preferences and identify a suitable support pathway.

Appropriate Practitioner Matching

We connect you with clinical psychologists, general psychologists, social workers, or counsellors whose training and scope of practice align with perinatal and trauma-informed care.

Coordinated Care

Where appropriate and with your consent, practitioners can liaise with your GP, obstetrician, midwife, or child health nurse.

Practical Referral Support

Our team assists with GP referral requirements, Mental Health Treatment Plans, and Medicare-related paperwork where applicable.

Flexible Access

In-person appointments are available at our Brisbane clinics in Toowong and Manly West, alongside secure Online Therapy / Telehealth Australia-wide where clinically appropriate, making it easier to attend sessions around baby's routine.

Start with a Conversation

You Don't Have to Carry Your Birth Story Alone

You may not be sure whether what you are experiencing is birth trauma, postnatal anxiety, or exhaustion, or how to begin talking about what happened.

If pregnancy or birth left you feeling shaken, unheard, or overwhelmed and you would like a warm, non-judgmental space to talk things through, reaching out can be a helpful first step.

Share only as much as feels comfortable, and our team will help you explore an appropriate pathway forward.

Contact Michelle Barratt Psychology on (07) 3185 0040 or reach out via our online contact form to learn more about perinatal and trauma therapy support.
